messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raúl had always taken pride in being composed, a prosecutor who could sit through grim testimony without flinching, but after the assault that occurred late one winter evening outside his apartment building, that steadiness began to fracture. He had been returning home alone when a man he knew from the neighborhood approached him under the pretense of a friendly exchange, and the betrayal of a familiar face made the attack feel all the more inescapable. In the months that followed, certain moments seized him without warning: being around children on the courthouse steps, where their voices and small bodies seemed to sharpen his dread; a particular coldness on his skin from winter air or air conditioning that carried him straight back to the physical helplessness of that night; and encounters with related people, especially acquaintances who resembled the assailant in face or manner, which could make his stomach turn before he had fully registered why. When those cues hit, the memory did not arrive as a story he could tell from a distance. It came back with almost unbearable clarity, every detail intact — the angle of the streetlight, the pressure of the pavement, the smell of the man’s jacket — and it forced its way into his mind as if the event were happening again in the present tense. What distressed him most was that these intrusions seemed to confirm what he had already come to believe about himself: that he was dirty, contaminated, and somehow permanently damaged, his body no longer fully his own. Because of that, he began to feel that the world itself was dangerous, and he could not trust even ordinary surroundings not to turn against him. Raúl started scanning exits the moment he entered any room or building, noticing knives in restaurant kitchens, heavy tools in garages, anything that might be used as a weapon, and he avoided unfamiliar places altogether because he felt unable to assess the danger quickly enough. The more he judged the world as perilous and himself as physically compromised, the more vigilant he became, and that vigilance made the old images easier to catch and harder to shake. A crowded hallway, a child brushing past him in the courthouse, the sudden chill of conditioned air across his forearms — each could pull the memory back in with such force that it again seemed immediate, which in turn flooded him with the conviction that he was unsafe and irrevocably altered. He then redoubled his attention to exits and objects that could harm him, and he became even more sensitive to the same kinds of cues, watching for children, familiar men, and changes in temperature before they could surprise him. Over time this left him more restricted in daily life; he declined invitations to unfamiliar neighborhoods, took longer routes to work, and stayed on edge during routine hearings, all while telling himself that caution was the only thing preventing another violation. At 67, widowed and living alone, he finally sought help when he noticed that even arriving at court in the morning could set off the same rapid cycle of intrusion, dread, and self-disgust, and he was afraid not only that the memories would keep ambushing him, but that he would continue shrinking his life around them.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows negative appraisals increasing vigilance and threat, but it does not clearly say those beliefs caused the specific triggers/cues (children, cold air, familiar men) to appear or become activated.
The vignette shows threat leading to scanning and avoidance, but it does not clearly state that the sense of danger directly brought the traumatic memory back in.
